'''''Ammi majus''''', commonly called  '''bishop's flower''', '''false bishop's weed''', '''laceflower''', '''bullwort''', etc., is a member of the carrot family [[Apiaceae]]. The plant, which has white lace-like flower clusters, has a large distribution through [[Southern Europe]], [[North Africa]] and [[West Asia|West]] and [[Central Asia|Central]] Asia, though it is hypothesized to be native to the [[Nile River]] Valley.

==Nomenclature==

The plant<ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN|access-date = 8 January 2018}}</ref> is called by various [[Common names (plants)|common names]]: bishop's flower<ref name="quattrocchi"/><ref name="walliser"/><ref name="taylor"/> or [[bishop's weed]]{{Refn|name="lazarides&hince-grin"}} (false bishop's weed{{Refn|name="erhardt-grin"}});{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|"bishop's weed" being an ambiguous name that could be confused with ''[[Aegopodium podagraria]]''.<ref name="walliser"/>}} laceflower,{{Refn|name="hanelt-grin"}}<ref name="walliser"/><ref name="taylor"/> '''lady's lace'''<ref name="walliser"/> or '''false Queen Anne's lace''';<ref name="quattrocchi"/><ref name="walliser"/>{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|As opposed to the true "Queen Anne's lace" (''[[Daucus carota]]'').<ref name="walliser"/>}} bullwort{{Refn|name="stace"}}<ref name="walliser"/> ('''large bullwort''');<ref name="quattrocchi"/> '''white dill'''<ref name="taylor"/> and '''greater ammi'''.{{Refn|name="rehm-grin"}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Other common names listed are: '''crow's foot'''; '''devil's carrot'''; '''herb william'''; '''honey plant'''; '''mayweed'''.<ref name="quattrocchi"/>}}

It is known in Arabic as ''hirz al-shayateen'' ({{lang|ar|حِرز الشياطين}}) or ''khella/khilla shaitani'' ({{lang|ar|خلة شیطانی}}),<ref name="quattrocchi"/> meaning, respectively, 'Devil's Amulet/Refuge' and 'Devil's Toothpick-weed.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

The plant has also been introduced into China, where it is called ''da a min qin'' ({{lang-zh|大阿米芹}}) and cultivated in medicinal farms.<ref name="she&watson"/><ref name="quattrocchi"/>

==Description==
''Ammi majus'' is a [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] annual,<ref name="walliser"/><ref name="she&watson"/> or rather a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] that behaves like an annual in cultivation.{{sfnp|Niir|2006|p=266}}

The lower leaves are 1-2-pinnate, upper leaves 2(-3)-pinnate with serrate lobes.{{Refn|name="stace"}}

The inflorescence is compound [[umbel]];<ref name="quattrocchi"/> they are white umbrella-shaped flowers like those of Queen Anne's lace,<ref name="walliser"/> blooming June–July and fruiting July–August.<ref name="she&watson"/>

== Distribution ==
Considered indigenous to Egypt,{{sfnp|Niir|2006|p=265}} or parts of Europe and the Middle East/West Asia.<ref name="walliser"/><ref name="quattrocchi"/> It is also found scattered in the British Isles, in North and Central Scotland,{{Refn|name="stace"}} widely distributed in the Mediterranean region (including Southern Europe{{Refn|name="stace"}} and North Africa<ref name="quattrocchi"/>), as well as West Africa and [[Abyssinia]].{{sfnp|Niir|2006|p=265}}

==Uses==
In Egypt around 2000 BC, the juice of ''Ammi majus'' was rubbed on patches of [[vitiligo]]<ref name="Marshall-2006">{{cite journal | last=Marshall | first=Scott R | title=Technology Insight: ECP for the treatment of GvHD—can we offer selective immune control without generalized immunosuppression? | journal=[[Nature Clinical Practice Oncology]] | publisher=[[Nature Publishing]] | volume=3 | issue=6 | year=2006 | issn=1743-4254 | doi=10.1038/ncponc0511 | pages=302–314| pmid=16757968 }}</ref> after which patients were encouraged to lie in the sun.<ref name="McGovern and Barkley 2000">{{cite journal |journal=The Electronic Textbook of Dermatology |url=http://telemedicine.org/botanica/bot1.htm |title=Botanical Dermatology |last1=McGovern |first1=Thomas W |last2=Barkley |first2=Theodore M |at=Section Phytophotodermatitis |publisher=Internet Dermatology Society |date=2000 |volume=37 |issue=5 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-4362.1998.00385.x |pmid=9620476 |s2cid=221810453 |access-date=October 7, 2018|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In the 13th century, vitiligo was treated with a tincture of honey and the powdered seeds of a plant called "aatrillal," which was abundant in the Nile River Valley. The plant has since been identified as ''A. majus'',<ref>{{cite book |author1=Wyss, P. |editor1-last=Wyss |editor1-first=P. |editor2-last=Tadir |editor2-first=Y. |editor3-last=Tromberg |editor3-first=B. J. |editor4-last=Haller |editor4-first=U. |title=Photomedicine in Gynecology and Reproduction |date=2000 |publisher=Karger |location=Basel |pages=4–11 |url=https://www.karger.com/Article/Pdf/62800 |chapter=History of Photomedicine|doi=10.1159/000062800 |isbn=3-8055-6905-X }}</ref> but the trade name Aatrillal is still used today to refer to the yellowish-brown powder made from its seeds.

''Ammi majus'' contains significant amounts of [[furanocoumarins]] [[bergapten]] and xanthotoxin (also known as [[methoxsalen]]), two [[psoralen]] derivatives well known for their photosensitizing effects. Indeed, ''A. majus'' may well be the world's major source of methoxsalen.<ref name="McGovern and Barkley 2000" />

The practice of using ''Ammi majus'' to treat vitiligo implicitly acknowledges the [[hyperpigmentation]] effects caused by exposure to a photosensitizing agent (such as methoxsalen) followed by ultraviolet radiation. An excess of either the photosensitizing agent or subsequent UV exposure can lead to [[phytophotodermatitis]],<ref name="McGovern and Barkley 2000" /><ref name="Alouani et al. 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Alouani |first1=I. |last2=Fihmi |first2=N. |last3=Zizi |first3=N. |last4=Dikhaye |first4=S. |title=Phytophotodermatitis following the use of ''Ammi Majus'' Linn (Bishop's weed) for vitiligo |journal=Our Dermatol. Online |date=2018 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=93–94 |doi=10.7241/ourd.20181.29 |url=http://www.odermatol.com/odermatology/20181/29.Phytophoto-ImaneA.pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref> a serious skin inflammation. Despite this danger, ''A. majus'' is cultivated for its furanocoumarins, which are still used for the treatment of skin disease, particularly the furanocoumarin xanthotoxin also known as "ammoidin" and by the brand name "Oxsoralen".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Ammi+majus|title=Plants For A Future: ''Ammi majus''}}</ref>{{sfnp|Niir|2006|pp=266–267}}

==Cultivation==
Like its close relative ''[[Ammi visnaga]]'', ''A. majus'' and its [[cultivar]]s are frequently seen in gardens where they are grown from seed annually. The species<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/25047/i-Ammi-majus-i/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Ammi majus''
| publisher=Royal Horticultural Society | date=2017 | access-date=12 January 2018}}</ref> and the cultivar 'Graceland'<ref name = RHSPF1>{{cite web 
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/255623/i-Ammi-majus-i-Graceland/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Ammi majus'' 'Graceland'
| publisher=Royal Horticultural Society | date=2017 | access-date=5 January 2018}}</ref>  
have both gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].
